title: Patient H.M. (1953)

youtube.title: Every Person He Met Was a Stranger. Forever. #Shorts
youtube.description:
You wake up after brain surgery. From now on, every new person you meet is a stranger, forever.
But your hands are about to remember something your mind can't.

This is the story of Henry Molaison, known to science as Patient H.M., told from the inside. After surgery for severe epilepsy in 1953 he could no longer form new long-term memories. Yet with psychologist Brenda Milner he got better at a mirror-drawing task over three days, with no memory of ever doing it.

What do YOUR hands remember that your mind forgot? Tell me in the comments.

Sources:
- Scoville, W. B., & Milner, B. (1957). Loss of recent memory after bilateral hippocampal lesions. Journal of Neurology, Neurosurgery & Psychiatry, 20(1), 11-21.
- Milner, B. (1962). Les troubles de la memoire accompagnant des lesions hippocampiques bilaterales.
- Corkin, S. (2013). Permanent Present Tense. Basic Books.

sources: Scoville & Milner (1957): in 1953 Henry Molaison, then 27, had parts of both medial temporal lobes removed (including much of the hippocampus) to treat severe epilepsy; afterwards he could not form new long-term memories of events and facts.
Corkin (2013), Permanent Present Tense: his seizures became much less frequent; researchers, including Brenda Milner, studied him for decades and he did not remember meeting them.
Milner (1962): in a mirror-drawing task (tracing a star seen only in a mirror) his performance improved steadily over three days, though each day he had no memory of having done it before.
lines: You wake up after brain surgery. From now on, every new person you meet will be a stranger. Forever.
Nineteen fifty-three. You're twenty-seven, and your seizures are so bad you can barely live a normal life. A surgeon offers an experimental operation.
He removes parts of both sides of your brain, deep inside. Afterwards, your seizures become much rarer.
But something else is gone. You can't make new memories. Meet someone, look away, and they're gone from your mind.
A psychologist studies you for decades. Every single time she walks into the room, you meet her for the first time.
She gives you a strange task: trace a star, but you can only see your hand in a mirror. It's very hard.
Over three days, you get better and better, almost perfect. And every day you swear you've never done it before.
Your mind forgot. Your hands remembered. Memory isn't one thing. Learning a skill runs on a different system in the brain.
You were Henry Molaison, known to science as H.M. What do your hands remember that your mind has forgotten?
